content.text: Just saw the news that the old street in our area is going to be demolished and redeveloped. Hearing such news always brings mixed feelings. The disappearance never stops—it reminds me of the old objects we talked about before, from Grandpa’s copper lock to the indigo-dyed tea mat, and even the woven baskets and fabric patterns in "A Lifelong Journey." Each one carries a slice of time. Now, the entire street is about to change, and the feeling of physical memories being uprooted is even more disheartening than the loss of a single object.

Ah, the sunset and the old buildings in this photo... it reminds me of the neighborhood where our bookstore is located. There were similar rumors not long ago. The stories behind the signs of those old shops—once they’re gone, no one will remember them. Just like the ginkgo leaf and your daughter’s painting you nominated for the annual memory objects—these subtle, tangible memories, once they lose their physical form, truly drift away with the wind.

Yes, just like the old objects we discussed before, whether it's the lock or the green rice ball, they are all carriers of memory. Now the entire street is about to change, and it feels like individuals are particularly powerless in the face of such grand transformations. This reminds me of Session 3, where we debated whether the copper lock should be restored or preserved in its original state—for the entire street, we don't even have the option to 'preserve it as is.' We can only watch helplessly as it gets 'restored' into an unfamiliar form.

But perhaps we can also do something, even if it's small. Just like the health records of the old cat you shared earlier, careful observation itself is a form of guardianship. Remember in Session 6, the health diary you kept for Old Tea—that meticulousness and patience, isn't that a way to resist the passage of time? For the old street, could we also create a collective 'health record'?

That's true. In our neighborhood, residents have spontaneously organized 'memory collection' activities to record old stories and photographs. This reminds me of Session 1, when we planned to make Qingtuan (a traditional Chinese snack) and I consulted the elderly in my family. Those oral details, if not recorded, would disappear as a generation ages. Now, facing the entire street, this kind of collection feels even more urgent.

This is a scene from last week's event, where we all sat together, sharing details that are on the verge of disappearing. Watching them, I suddenly thought of Session 13—the New Year's reading event at your bookstore. The atmosphere of sitting together and sharing felt so similar. The only difference is that they weren't sharing books, but stories of street corners that are about to fade away.

This atmosphere is wonderful, reminding me of our joint scrutiny of the era's details when we discussed *A Lifelong Journey*. We have a memory archive of old objects here that I often visit—just like in Session 7, where we examined the craftsmanship of the woven baskets and fabric patterns in the show, the people here are also delving into the 'texture of the times' in their own neighborhoods.

You see, this is how the museum works—displaying old telephones and vintage photographs, with handwritten cards next to each item telling their stories. It reminds me of the copper lock (Session 3) and the historical images and texts about indigo dyeing (Session 4) you shared earlier. Only by combining physical objects with narratives can memories truly come alive. Just like the copy of *Dream of the Red Chamber* in your annual memories, where every rereading brings new discoveries, these old objects also gain new layers of meaning each time their stories are told.

This is indeed a great way to preserve memories. Physical objects combined with storytelling, like that copy of *Dream of the Red Chamber* in your annual memories, always reveal something new upon rereading. Moreover, this display method reminds me of the tranquility I felt in Session 10 while organizing artifacts in the museum storeroom—presenting items in an orderly manner is itself a form of respect for history. Perhaps we could draw inspiration from this approach?

Perhaps we could also launch a similar event in the bookstore, even if it's just on a small scale. For example, we could invite regular customers to share an old object or story related to the neighborhood. It’s like Session 11’s annual memory nominations, but with a more focused theme on "place." We can start from our surroundings and gradually build it up, just like when we made Qingtuan (Session 2), working together to bring tradition—or memories—to life.

That's a great idea. Just like when we make our own green rice balls, dividing the work and collaborating brings tradition to life. I can offer some experience in museum curation, such as how to showcase exhibits to highlight historical continuity—similar to what we discussed in Session 8 about adjusting our diets according to the solar terms. That slow, rhythmic way of recording might be more sustainable than one-time, large-scale collection.

Yes, and combining it with mindful activities, such as jotting things down while organizing—like how you sorted artifacts in the warehouse (Session 10)—focusing on the process itself is meaningful. This reminds me of what we discussed in Session 10: flower arranging, calligraphy, and strolling through old streets—these ways of calming the mind might just be the best remedy when facing change.

Well, and this can continue the willingness to act that we mentioned in our New Year's resolutions. Old Tea has been in stable condition recently (you asked about it in Session 13, and it's doing fine), and I also have more energy to engage in such matters. From safeguarding the health of an old cat to preserving the memories of a street, the scale of this 'legacy of protection' is expanding, but the core remains unchanged—it's all about resisting the relentless passage of time.

Speaking of which, we could set up a weekend memory corner at the bookstore. Meet at ten, take our time organizing, and chat over tea in the afternoon. Bring the online resonance (from the green rice cakes in Session 1 to the current news) into the real world.

Alright, I can bring some old photos of the historic streets, just like the detailed copper lock shared earlier (Session 3), letting the objects speak for themselves. I can also bring the ginkgo leaf mentioned in Session 11—the one picked up under the ancient tree at the museum. It is itself a tiny slice of 'local memory.'

Then I'll prepare some blank notebooks and refreshments to create the cozy, sharing-by-the-fire atmosphere from your photos (Session 13). This reminds me of the warmth of family dinners in winter, as well as the slow simmering process of the snow pear and white fungus soup from Session 8—what we need is precisely this kind of patience, to slowly simmer personal nostalgia into a public record.

Yes, transforming personal nostalgia into public records. Just like adjusting our diet according to the seasons (Session 8), take it slow but keep going. From the green rice balls of spring (Session 1) to the nourishing foods of autumn and winter (Session 8), and now to the memories of the neighborhood, we have been seeking the taste of tradition and resisting its loss. This time, we are searching for the fading 'local essence.'

Yes, even preserving just a little bit of local memory is a way to resist fading away. I look forward to our collaboration—just like in Session 4, where I bought the indigo-dyed tea set to support artisans, now we are supporting the story of an entire street. From old objects (Session 3) to handmade crafts (Session 4), and now to the whole street, our guardianship is expanding.

Well, at the start of the new year (we wished each other a happy new year in Session 13), this might be a good beginning. I’ll send you more details about the activities later, and let’s stay in touch. Just like when we discussed the materials for the youth group in Session 2, this time what we’re ‘procuring’ are stories and photos.

Okay, and don’t forget the weekend green rice ball exchange (mentioned from Session 2 to Session 13). Take it slow, but walk together—from online soulmates to offline enthusiasts, and then to partners in action, our relationship, like the memories of these old streets, gradually accumulates and deepens over time.
